stated_availability: Section 4.2 (p. 7): "We used the IntCal20 curve for all models (Reimer et al., 2020) using the calibration process defined in equation [3]. All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942." Appendix A (p. 9): "Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2024.105962." Article-level licence (p. 1 footer): "0305-4403/(c) 2024 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)." No separate journal "Data availability" section is printed; no licence is stated in the paper for the deposited data/code themselves. (Descriptive record only; no L1-L6 level assigned.)

F1.evidence: Section 4.2, p. 7: 'All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942.' A Zenodo DOI (10.5281/zenodo.10782942) is a globally unique persistent identifier covering the data.

F2.evidence: Deposit is DOI-registered on Zenodo, which necessarily carries DataCite-schema structured metadata (creators, title, publisher, publication year, resource type, description). The paper additionally supplies rich structured description of each dataset in Section 4.1 (sources, n, site counts, filtering thresholds, spatial/chronological windows).

F3.evidence: DOI registration entails that the DataCite/Zenodo metadata record itself contains the identifier 10.5281/zenodo.10782942 as its mandatory Identifier field; the paper cites the resolvable form 'https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942' (p. 7).

F4.evidence: Instrument F4: 'Resource indexed in searchable registry (Zenodo, CRAN, DataCite)'. The data are deposited on Zenodo ('permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942', p. 7), hence indexed in Zenodo search and the DataCite index; the live GitHub repository (github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve) is additionally searchable.

A1.evidence: Retrievable by DOI resolution over HTTPS from Zenodo and by HTTPS from GitHub (p. 7). Completeness rule satisfied: data_completeness coverage_category is 'substantial' (14/15 datasets Tier 0-2, 93.3%), not 'minimal' or 'partial', and the paper states the full analysis data (not merely a supplement subset) are deposited.

A1_1.evidence: Access is via open, free, universally implementable HTTPS/DOI resolution to Zenodo and GitHub; no login, subscription, or proprietary client is required ('available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942', p. 7).

A1_2.evidence: HTTPS as served by Zenodo and GitHub supports authentication/authorisation procedures where these are needed. No restriction is necessary for these data (published radiocarbon determinations, no human-subjects or CARE-relevant sensitivity), and none is imposed, so the 'where necessary' condition is met without gating.

A2.evidence: Deposit is on Zenodo (CERN-operated), which maintains the DataCite metadata record and DOI landing/tombstone page independently of file availability; the paper describes the deposit as 'permanently archived' (p. 7). GitHub alone would not satisfy this, but the Zenodo archive does.

I1.evidence: The deposited data are machine-readable inputs consumed directly by the archived R scripts ('All data and R scripts are available...', p. 7; models 'implemented using the NIMBLE ... probabilistic programming language in R ... and the nimbleCarbon R package', Section 4.2), i.e. structured tabular radiocarbon data (lab determination, error, site, taxon) rather than PDF/unstructured formats.

I2.evidence: No controlled vocabulary, ontology, thesaurus, or gazetteer with PIDs is cited or applied (no PeriodO, Getty AAT, CIDOC-CRM, ARIADNEplus, Dublin Core or equivalent). Taxa, materials, and periods are given in free-text disciplinary prose (e.g. 'chestnut, horse chestnut, walnut, and acorns', Section 4.1.2).

I3.evidence: Provenance links to source datasets are given only as prose bibliographic citations in the article (e.g. 'Japanese dates were collated from the radiocarbon database of Japan (Kudo et al., 2023) and the rice radiocarbon database used in (Crema et al., 2022)', Section 4.1.2). No evidence of typed, PID-based related identifiers ('isDerivedFrom [DOI]') in the deposited (meta)data; several cited source datasets carry no DOI in the reference list.

R1.evidence: Datasets are richly described with a plurality of relevant attributes in Section 4.1: 'We examined a total of 1479 14C dates on seed remains from Japan (n = 551, from 215 sites ...) and Britain (n = 928, from 314 sites ...)'; taxon-level breakdowns (rice n = 203, wild nuts n = 348, wheat n = 261, barley n = 130, hazelnut n = 537), burial dates (cremation n = 1417, inhumation n = 1119), plus Fig. 1 site distribution maps.

R1_1.evidence: Deposit is an open Zenodo record, for which a licence selection is mandatory and is exposed as machine-readable rights metadata (the pulled FAIR guide scores this scenario 'R1.1: 1 point (licence captured in Zenodo metadata)'). Caveat recorded: the only licence stated in the paper itself is article-level - 'This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)' (p. 1) and CC BY applied to the Author Accepted Manuscript (Acknowledgements, p. 9) - no artefact-specific licence statement appears in the text.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed provenance documented: named upstream sources per case study (Section 4.1.2-4.1.3), explicit transformation and filtering rules ('dates with a cumulative calibrated probability mass equal to or larger than 0.5 for the interval 4000-1700 cal BP', 'excluded the island of Hokkaido and the Ryukyuan islands', 'a higher probability threshold (0.99 instead of 0.5) to avoid any edge effects'), calibration curve stated ('We used the IntCal20 curve for all models'), derivation scripts archived, and CRediT 'Data curation' assigned to all four authors (p. 9).

R1_3.evidence: No domain data standard or domain repository is applied to the deposit: data are placed in a general-purpose repository (Zenodo/GitHub) rather than tDAR, Open Context, or an ARIADNEplus-aligned service, and no discipline metadata schema, data dictionary standard, or radiocarbon reporting standard is cited for the deposited files. Disciplinary convention (CRA + error, IntCal20, cal BP) is followed in the analysis but no community standard is documented as applied to the dataset.

F1.evidence: Section 4.2, p. 7: 'All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942.' The R scripts carry the Zenodo DOI as a persistent identifier (not a bare GitHub URL).

F2.evidence: Zenodo DOI registration entails DataCite-schema structured metadata (creators, title, publisher, publication year, resource type, description) for the archived code release; the article supplies additional structured description of what the code implements (equations 5-12, priors, MCMC settings, Section 4.2).

F3.evidence: The archived code's DataCite/Zenodo metadata record carries the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10782942 as its mandatory Identifier field; the paper cites the resolvable form (p. 7).

F4.evidence: Instrument F4: indexed in a searchable registry (Zenodo, CRAN, DataCite). The code snapshot is archived on Zenodo and thereby indexed by Zenodo and DataCite; the live repository github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve is additionally searchable.

A1.evidence: Code retrievable by DOI resolution over HTTPS from Zenodo and by HTTPS/git from GitHub (p. 7). Source scripts (R), not compiled binaries.

A1_1.evidence: HTTPS/DOI resolution to Zenodo and GitHub: open, free, universally implementable; no registration, subscription, or proprietary tooling required. Runtime (R, NIMBLE, nimbleCarbon) is itself free and open.

A1_2.evidence: Zenodo and GitHub implement authentication/authorisation procedures where needed; no restriction is necessary or imposed for this code, so the 'where necessary' condition is satisfied without gating.

A2.evidence: Code is archived on Zenodo, which retains the DataCite metadata record and DOI landing page even if files become unavailable; the paper describes the archive as permanent ('permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942', p. 7). GitHub alone would not satisfy A2.

I1.evidence: Code is in R, an open, formal, broadly implemented language, using declared open packages: 'Both the hierarchical model described in equations [5-6] and the random walk ICAR model were implemented using the NIMBLE (de Valpine et al., 2017, 2020) probabilistic programming language in R (R Core Team, 2020) and the nimbleCarbon R package (Crema, 2022b)' (Section 4.2).

I2.evidence: No software metadata vocabulary or standard is evidenced (no CodeMeta.json, CITATION.cff, or SPDX/ontology-backed descriptors cited in the paper); dependency naming is ad hoc prose citation.

I3.evidence: Dependencies are cited bibliographically in the article (NIMBLE with a Zenodo DOI in the reference list; nimbleCarbon; R Core Team 2020), but there is no evidence of typed, PID-based related identifiers within the code artefact or its deposit metadata (no lock file, DESCRIPTION-with-DOIs, or 'uses software [DOI]' relations demonstrated).

R1.evidence: Analysis is richly documented for reuse: full model specification (equations 5-12), explicit priors ('r ~ Exponential(100)', 'mu ~ Beta(2,2)', 'phi ~ Gamma(5,0.1)'), truncated normal for m with stated means/SDs, and sampler settings - 'four chains, each with 1 million iterations (half discarded as burn-in) and with thinning set to 50', ICAR run with 'four chains, each with 100,000 iterations (20,000 of which were discarded for burn-in), with parameters collected every four steps' - plus convergence diagnostics (Gelman-Rubin, Rhat reported in Table 1).

R1_1.evidence: The code is deposited as an open Zenodo record, for which a machine-readable licence is a mandatory, exposed metadata field (pulled FAIR guide, GitHub+Zenodo scenario: 'R1.1: 1 point (licence captured in Zenodo metadata)'). Caveat: the paper states no licence for the scripts themselves; its licence statements are article-level CC BY 4.0 (p. 1) and CC BY applied to the Author Accepted Manuscript (p. 9).

R1_2.evidence: Provenance of the software contribution is documented: CRediT assigns 'Software' and 'Formal analysis' to E.R. Crema (p. 9); code is version-controlled on GitHub with a citable archived snapshot on Zenodo (p. 7); the computational workflow (data filtering, calibration with IntCal20, model fitting, posterior predictive checks with '1000 randomly selected parameters from the joint posterior distributions') is described step-by-step in Sections 4.1-4.2.

R1_3.evidence: Meets domain community standards for computational archaeology (Marwick-style compendium practice): code and data archived together under a DOI, and independently reviewed for reproducibility - Acknowledgements, p. 9: 'We thank the two reviewers ... and Ben Marwick for reviewing the computational code and providing suggestions to improve its reproducibility.' Analysis is built on a released, citable R package (nimbleCarbon, Crema 2022b) in the R ecosystem.

barriers: Closed monograph/edited volume (Tier 3): Healy 2012, chapter in 'Is There a British Chalcolithic?' (Prehistoric Society Research Paper, Oxbow Books) - one of eight upstream sources for the case-study-2 burial dates; no open version indicated.
Paywalled journal articles requiring manual table extraction (Tier 2): Bloxam and Parker Pearson 2022 (Proc. Prehist. Soc.); Willis et al. 2016 (Antiquity).
Doctoral theses requiring manual extraction from institutional repositories (Tier 2): Bloxam 2020 (UCL); Wilkin 2013 (University of Birmingham).
Supplementary-table extraction from a subscription journal (Tier 2): Olalde et al. 2018 (Nature).

Mitigation recorded: the paper states 'All data and R scripts are available on https://github.com/ercrema/diffusionCurve and permanently archived on https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10782942' (Section 4.2, p. 7), so the compiled analysis-ready datasets (Japan seeds n=551/215 sites; Britain seeds n=928/314 sites; Britain burials cremation n=1417, inhumation n=1119; three simulated datasets) are Tier 0 and the Tier 2-3 upstream barriers do not block reproduction - they affect only independent re-derivation of the compilation.

Enumeration (Tier in brackets): 1-3 simulated datasets 1a/1b/2 generated by the archived scripts [0]; 4 Japanese 14C seed dates from the archaeological radiocarbon database of Japan, Kudo et al. 2023 [0]; 5 rice radiocarbon database of Crema et al. 2022 [0]; 6 British 14C seed dates from Bevan et al. 2017 [0]; 7 compiled British burial 14C dataset as deposited [0]; 8 Bloxam 2020 [2]; 9 Bloxam and Parker Pearson 2022 [2]; 10 Healy 2012 [3]; 11 Mallick and Reich 2023 AADR, DOI 10.7910/DVN/FFIDCW [0]; 12 Olalde et al. 2018 [2]; 13 Wilkin 2013 [2]; 14 Willis et al. 2016 [2]; 15 IntCal20 calibration curve, Reimer et al. 2020 [0]. Record-weighted coverage is higher still (>95%), since the large majority of dates come from Tier 0 sources (Japan database, Bevan et al. 2017).

Assessment limitation: supplementary files and the Zenodo/GitHub deposits were deliberately not provided for this scoring pass, so tiers are assigned from the paper's own statements and content as instructed, not from retrieval attempts.
